# ForkJoinPool

The `ForkJoinPool` is a specialised thread pool for divide-and-conquer work: a
task recursively splits into smaller, independent subtasks. Its work-stealing
scheduler allows a worker with no local work to take a queued task from another
worker, which can help balance uneven computations.

The following example shows the mechanics by summing an array of integers. Its
log can show leaf tasks on different workers, but it neither proves that a steal
occurred nor measures a performance improvement.

A sequential loop is the baseline: it produces the same result without splitting
work. The example does not time either approach, because an array of 1,000
values with logging is too small and noisy to support a performance conclusion.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- explain recursive splitting, work stealing, and result joining;
- distinguish `invoke()` from submitting tasks before joining them;
- explain how task completion makes the array updates visible; and
- identify overhead, blocking, and task-size trade-offs.

## Prerequisite

- [Oracle Java 21](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

## The program to inspect

`Main` compares a sequential sum with a `RecursiveTask` invoked on a dedicated
pool. Each pool is closed by try-with-resources: closing initiates an orderly
shutdown and waits for termination.

```java
logSection("Sum array content (sequential)");
final long sequentialResult = sumSequentially(createArray(1_000));
log("Sum of the array: " + sequentialResult);

logSection("Sum array content (invoke())");
log("Use invoke() to sum all the array's content using a RecursiveTask");
try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool()) {
    log("Invoke the sum recursive task");
    final int[] numbers = createArray(1_000);
    final long result = pool.invoke(SumRecursiveTask.of(numbers));
    log("Sum of the array: " + result);
}
```

The `RecursiveTask` sums a range directly when it has at most 100 elements.
Otherwise it forks the left range, computes the right range, joins the left
result, and combines both sums. Ranges use an inclusive start and exclusive end.

```java
package demo;

import java.io.Serial;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;

public final class SumRecursiveTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {

    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = -1L;

    private static final int THRESHOLD = 100; /* Task size threshold */
    private final int[] numbers;
    private final int start;
    private final int end;

    public static RecursiveTask<Long> of(final int[] numbers) {
        return new SumRecursiveTask(numbers, 0, numbers.length);
    }

    private SumRecursiveTask(final int[] numbers, final int start, final int end) {
        this.numbers = numbers;
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    @Override
    protected Long compute() {
        /* If the task is small enough, compute directly */
        if (end - start <= THRESHOLD) {
            log("Compute the sum between indices [" + start + "] and [" + end + ']');
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = start; i < end; i++) {
                sum += numbers[i];
            }
            return sum;
        }

        /* Split the task into two subtasks */
        final int middle = (start + end) / 2;
        final SumRecursiveTask leftTask = new SumRecursiveTask(numbers, start, middle);
        final SumRecursiveTask rightTask = new SumRecursiveTask(numbers, middle, end);

        /* Fork the subtasks and join their results */
        leftTask.fork(); /* Asynchronously execute the left task */
        final long rightResult = rightTask.compute(); /* Compute the right task */
        final long leftResult = leftTask.join(); /* Wait for the left task */

        /* Combine the results */
        return leftResult + rightResult;
    }
}
```

`invoke()` submits one task and waits for its result. `submit()` instead returns
a `ForkJoinTask` immediately. This lets the caller queue two independent sums
before choosing when to `join()` their results. Submitting both tasks does not
guarantee that they will run at the same time; the pool decides how its workers
execute and steal work.

```java
logSection("Sum two arrays (submit())");
log("Use submit() to queue two RecursiveTasks before waiting for their results");
try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool()) {
    final ForkJoinTask<Long> firstSum = pool.submit(SumRecursiveTask.of(createArray(1_000)));
    final ForkJoinTask<Long> secondSum = pool.submit(SumRecursiveTask.of(createArray(500)));
    log("Both sum tasks submitted");
    final long result = firstSum.join() + secondSum.join();
    log("Sum of both arrays: " + result);
}
```

A `RecursiveAction` follows the same splitting pattern when no result needs to
be returned. Each leaf increments a disjoint range of the shared array. Once
`invoke()` returns, all subtasks have completed, so the first and last values
show the completed mutation. Each non-leaf task uses `invokeAll()` to fork and
join its children before completing. The `ForkJoinTask` completion methods
provide the visibility needed for the joining task to observe completed changes;
the completion chain carries them back to the caller of `pool.invoke()`. Each
join orders the completed child’s actions before its parent continues. The Java
Memory Model governs that visibility and ordering. Disjoint ranges avoid
concurrent writes to the same elements; completion does not make overlapping
increments atomic. Neither log order nor a successful run proves visibility.

```java
logSection("Increment array content (invoke())");
log("Use RecursiveAction to increment the array's content using a RecursiveAction");
try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool()) {
    log("Invoke the increment recursive action");
    final int[] numbers = createArray(1_000);
    pool.invoke(IncrementRecursiveAction.of(numbers));
    log("First array value: " + numbers[0]);
    log("Last array value: " + numbers[numbers.length - 1]);
}
```

The action splits and joins ranges in `IncrementRecursiveAction`:

```java
package demo;

import java.io.Serial;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveAction;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;

public final class IncrementRecursiveAction extends RecursiveAction {

    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = -1L;

    private static final int THRESHOLD = 100;
    private final int[] numbers;
    private final int start;
    private final int end;

    public static RecursiveAction of(final int[] numbers) {
        return new IncrementRecursiveAction(numbers, 0, numbers.length);
    }

    private IncrementRecursiveAction(final int[] numbers, final int start, final int end) {
        this.numbers = numbers;
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    @Override
    protected void compute() {
        if (end - start <= THRESHOLD) {
            log("Increment values between indices [" + start + "] and [" + end + ']');
            for (int i = start; i < end; i++) {
                numbers[i]++;
            }
            return;
        }

        final int middle = (start + end) / 2;
        invokeAll(new IncrementRecursiveAction(numbers, start, middle),
                new IncrementRecursiveAction(numbers, middle, end));
    }
}
```

**When it fits**:

- Use it for sufficiently coarse, independent, CPU-bound work such as parallel
  array processing or recursive algorithms.
- `RecursiveTask` and `RecursiveAction` express splitting and joining without
  creating and coordinating threads directly.

**Trade-offs**:

- Splitting, scheduling, and combining work have a cost. This small, heavily
  logged array example demonstrates the API; it is not a benchmark and may be
  slower than a sequential loop.
- The threshold is workload-dependent: tasks that are too small add overhead,
  while tasks that are too large leave too little work to distribute.
- Avoid ordinary blocking I/O in a fork/join computation. Blocked workers reduce
  the pool’s capacity; use an executor intended for blocking work, or managed
  blocking when it is genuinely necessary.
